analysis.one_liner: Overrode courts and agencies to force completion of one named natural gas pipeline in Virginia and West Virginia.
analysis.headline: The bill got a hearing referral but never a vote; it died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress, while the pipeline it targeted was finished anyway under a separate law signed in June 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have had Congress declare that every federal permit and approval for the Mountain Valley Pipeline is valid, ordered the Army, Agriculture, and Interior departments to issue any remaining permits within 21 days, and barred anyone — including landowners already in court — from challenging those approvals in most courts. It was written for a single, already partly-built gas pipeline project. It was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, and no further action ever came.
analysis.who_benefits: The companies that own and are building the Mountain Valley Pipeline, and natural gas producers who would gain a new route to Eastern markets. The bill would have handed them what years of permitting fights and lawsuits had delayed: guaranteed permits and no way for opponents to sue. Landowners and communities along the route would not have been directly compensated; they would have lost their day in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The pipeline's owners and gas producers

how_it_helps.text: Congress would ratify every permit, biological opinion, and approval already issued for the pipeline, making them valid by statute regardless of pending litigation.

The Army, Agriculture, and Interior departments would have 21 days to issue every remaining permit, amend the Jefferson National Forest plan, and grant rights-of-way, on the specific terms the bill dictates.
No federal or state approval for the pipeline could be challenged in court; lawsuits already pending would be dismissed, with only the D.C. Circuit able to hear claims that the law itself is invalid.
The bill states its terms supersede any conflicting statute, regulation, or judicial decision.

analysis.who_pays: Landowners along the route and residents of affected communities, who would lose the ability to contest water, forest, and property impacts in court; taxpayers indirectly, through agencies whose environmental reviews would be overruled by statute; and anyone counting on courts to check agency decisions for this project.

drawbacks.text: Stripping judicial review for a single private project sets a precedent: Congress can pick a company's fight, bless its permits, and close the courthouse, leaving affected landowners and towns no legal remedy for water and property harm.

The bill's own economic claims — lower gas prices and reduced emissions — were contested; natural gas pipelines can also displace renewables and lock in fossil fuel infrastructure for decades, and critics said the project's demand case was overstated.
Forcing permits on a 21-day clock regardless of conditions on the ground would remove the safety valve agencies use when construction, stream crossings, or landslides create new hazards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to one pipeline consortium and gas producers; the costs — loss of court access, unreviewable permits, and whatever environmental harm occurs — fall on landowners and communities along the 300-mile route. There is no broad public benefit that plausibly offsets the precedent of Congress overriding courts for a named company.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee and subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2025, never reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Introduced May 18, 2023 by Rep. John Joyce with five original cosponsors, and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Natural Resources, and Agriculture committees.
Referred to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials subcommittee (May 19) and the Forestry subcommittee (June 23); no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed.

The same result the bill sought was achieved through a different route: the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, the debt-limit law signed June 3, 2023, included a provision statutorily approving the Mountain Valley Pipeline's permits, and construction finished in 2024.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no one gained from it directly — but the pipeline's owners still got what it wanted, through the debt-limit law instead. Landowners' court challenges were cut off either way.

for.name: Rep. John Joyce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to force pipeline completion and strip court review.

for.name: 11 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

for.name: Mountain Valley Pipeline joint venture partners
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for federal legislation ratifying their permits while litigation stalled the project.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters on record were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill died without either chamber voting, so there was no roll call to measure the split.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline developers (Mountain Valley Pipeline joint venture)
industries.note: The bill existed to hand one consortium guaranteed permits and immunity from lawsuits over a roughly $6 billion project that litigation had stalled. Its gain is landowners' and river communities' loss of any forum to contest harm.
The pipeline opens a route to Eastern and Southeast markets for gas producers in West Virginia and Pennsylvania, expanding their sales; consumers see only indirect, uncertain price effects.

industries.industry: Landowners and communities along the route
industries.note: They would lose the ability to challenge stream crossings, forest amendments, and property takings in any court; pending lawsuits would be dismissed.
Congress would overrule agencies' own records of decision on a fixed 21-day clock, cutting courts out of checking federal environmental decisions for this project.
